summary.text: Letting $d$ be the digit sum of $n$, factor off its $2$- and $5$-parts so that $d\mid 10^P d'$ with $(d',10)=1$; the congruence $n\equiv d\pmod 9$ ensures that one can choose $a$ with $9a\equiv10n\pmod{d'}$. Taking equal-length decimal blocks representing either $1$ or $10$, with $a$ blocks of the first kind and $n-a$ of the second, produces a number $V$ with digit sum $n$ and $d'\mid V$; multiplying $V$ by a sufficiently large power of $10$ then gives a positive number distinct from $n$ whose digit sum divides $n$ and which is divisible by $d$.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(x)\) denote the sum of the base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
This will imply that the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty, and hence that \(a(n)\ne0\).

We first record two elementary facts about decimal digit lists. We write digit lists in least-significant-digit-first order. Thus, if
\[
L=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{r-1}),
\]
then the integer represented by \(L\) is
\[
\operatorname{val}(L)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}x_i10^i.
\]

First, if every \(x_i\) lies in \(\{0,1,\ldots,9\}\), then
\[
D(\operatorname{val}(L))=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}x_i. \tag{1}
\]
This remains true when the list has zeros at its most significant end. Indeed, deleting such terminal zeros does not change either the represented integer or the sum of the entries. After they are deleted, the list is either empty, in which case both sides are zero, or it is the usual base-10 expansion of its value. Equation (1) then follows from uniqueness of the decimal expansion.

Second, suppose a list is formed by concatenating blocks \(b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_{s-1}\), each of the same length \(W\). If \(v_j=\operatorname{val}(b_j)\), then
\[
\operatorname{val}(b_0b_1\cdots b_{s-1})
 =\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}v_j10^{jW}. \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, for any positive modulus \(m\) satisfying
\[
10^W\equiv1\pmod m,
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname{val}(b_0b_1\cdots b_{s-1})
 \equiv\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}v_j\pmod m. \tag{3}
\]

Now fix \(n>0\), and put
\[
d=D(n).
\]
Because \(n\) is positive, its decimal expansion contains a nonzero digit, so \(d>0\). We also have
\[
d\le n. \tag{4}
\]
To see this, write \(n=\sum_i c_i10^i\) using its decimal digits. Since \(10^i\ge1\),
\[
n=\sum_i c_i10^i\ge\sum_i c_i=d.
\]

We next separate from \(d\) the factors that are not coprime to 10. Write
\[
d=2^\alpha5^\beta d',
\]
where \(d'>0\) is divisible by neither 2 nor 5. Thus
\[
\gcd(10,d')=1,
\qquad d'\mid d.
\]
If \(P=\max(\alpha,\beta)\), then
\[
d=2^\alpha5^\beta d'\mid 2^P5^P d'=10^P d'. \tag{5}
\]
Only these properties of \(d'\) and \(P\) will be needed.

We now seek an integer \(a\) satisfying
\[
0\le a<d'
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
9a\equiv10n\pmod{d'}. \tag{6}
\]
We verify that this congruence is soluble. Let
\[
g=\gcd(9,d').
\]
Every integer is congruent modulo 9 to the sum of its decimal digits, so
\[
n\equiv d\pmod9. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(g\mid9\), (7) also gives \(n\equiv d\pmod g\). On the other hand, \(g\mid d'\) and \(d'\mid d\), so \(g\mid d\). It follows that \(g\mid n\).

This is exactly the condition needed to solve (6). For completeness, write \(n=gt\), and use Bezout's identity to choose integers \(u,v\) such that
\[
g=9u+d'v.
\]
Multiplying by \(10t\) gives
\[
10n=9(10ut)+d'(10vt),
\]
so \(9(10ut)\equiv10n\pmod{d'}\). Let \(a\) be the least nonnegative residue of \(10ut\) modulo \(d'\). Then (6) holds. Moreover,
\[
a<d'\le d\le n, \tag{8}
\]
so both \(a\) and \(n-a\) are nonnegative integers.

Because \(10\) and \(d'\) are coprime, Euler's theorem gives
\[
10^{\varphi(d')}\equiv1\pmod{d'},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. Set
\[
W=2\varphi(d').
\]
Since \(d'>0\), \(\varphi(d')\ge1\), so \(W\ge2\). Squaring the congruence from Euler's theorem gives
\[
10^W\equiv1\pmod{d'}. \tag{9}
\]

We use two decimal blocks of length \(W\). In least-significant-digit-first notation, define
\[
A=(1,0,0,\ldots,0)
\]
and
\[
B=(0,1,0,\ldots,0).
\]
The condition \(W\ge2\) ensures that both are well-defined blocks of length \(W\). Their represented values and their sums of digits are
\[
\operatorname{val}(A)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{val}(B)=10,
\qquad
\sum A=\sum B=1. \tag{10}
\]

Form a list \(L\) by concatenating \(a\) copies of \(A\), followed by \(n-a\) copies of \(B\), and let
\[
V=\operatorname{val}(L).
\]
There are exactly \(n\) blocks in \(L\), and each block has digit sum 1. Therefore the sum of all entries of \(L\) is \(n\). Every entry of \(L\) is either 0 or 1, so (1) applies and gives
\[
D(V)=n. \tag{11}
\]
In particular, because \(n>0\), the list contains a digit 1, and hence
\[
V>0. \tag{12}
\]

We next prove that \(d'\mid V\). By (3), (9), and (10),
\[
V\equiv a\cdot1+(n-a)\cdot10
   =a+10(n-a)
   =10n-9a
   \pmod{d'}.
\]
The congruence defining \(a\) in (6) says precisely that \(10n-9a\equiv0\pmod{d'}\). Consequently,
\[
d'\mid V. \tag{13}
\]

It remains to restore the powers of 2 and 5 that were removed from \(d\). Set
\[
Q=P+n+1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
k=10^Q V.
\]
Clearly \(k>0\) by (12). From (5) and (13),
\[
d\mid10^P d'\mid10^P V.
\]
Since \(Q\ge P\), the number \(10^P V\) divides \(10^Q V=k\). Thus
\[
D(n)=d\mid k. \tag{14}
\]

Multiplication of a positive integer by \(10^Q\) merely appends \(Q\) zeros to its ordinary decimal expansion and therefore does not change its digit sum. Using (11), we obtain
\[
D(k)=D(10^Q V)=D(V)=n. \tag{15}
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
D(k)=n\mid n. \tag{16}
\]
Thus (14) and (16) are the two required mutual divisibility conditions.

We must also check that the constructed partner is distinct from \(n\). Since \(V\ge1\),
\[
k=10^Q V\ge10^Q.
\]
The elementary inequality \(n<2^n\) holds for every nonnegative integer \(n\), and \(Q=P+n+1\ge n\). Hence
\[
n<2^n\le2^Q\le10^Q\le k.
\]
Therefore \(k>n\), in particular \(k\ne n\).

We have now shown that for every \(n>0\) there exists a \(k\) satisfying
\[
k>0,
\qquad k\ne n,
\qquad D(n)\mid k,
\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
Let
\[
S_n=\{k\in\mathbb N:k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}.
\]
The construction proves that \(S_n\) is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it therefore has a least element, and this least element belongs to \(S_n\), so it is positive. By definition, when \(S_n\) is nonempty, \(a(n)\) is exactly this least element; the value 0 is used only when \(S_n\) is empty. Hence for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
a(n)>0,
\]
and in particular \(a(n)\ne0\), as claimed.
